title: ASML chief: ‘There is only one company making those machines’
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026

Anyone worried about the short-termism of the technology sector, the bravado of so many tech bros and the easy prickability of the AI bubble should take a reality-check trip to Veldhoven, the unremarkable Dutch municipality that is home to Europe’s biggest company.

ASML, arguably the most consequential yet low-profile company in the AI ecosystem, employs nearly half the town (population: 47,902) and another 25,000 besides, doing the no-nonsense work of making and marketing the ever-larger machines that churn out ever-smaller computer chips.

As for the company’s chief executive, Christophe Fouquet, a tech bro he most certainly is not. This grounded French physicist is both a refreshing antidote to the salesmen of Silicon Valley and a more convincing advocate for the durability of technological advance.

The secret of this 42-year-old company’s success, Fouquet tells me in a nondescript meeting room at ASML’s headquarters, has been teamwork. “If I had to summarise it, this has been a lot about extreme co-operation with the ecosystem, which is, first, our customers, but also our supply chain,” he explains, portraying ASML as the epitome of the collaborative European company, in stark contrast to a thrusting American one.

ASML, though still unknown by many people outside the tech sector, is an increasingly crucial linchpin in the global manufacture of chips. It has an extraordinary share of the market for chipmaking lithography machines, including a total monopoly on the most advanced extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, machines that are essential in the manufacture of chips for complex AI applications.

A new regular Monday interview featuring the biggest names in global finance and business. From the power brokers shaping the City to the international CEOs steering trade and industry, it will bring readers inside the companies and characters that matter most.

“I think there’s been a bit of a catch-up moment for a large part of the world, how a few companies have become critical for the future of the entire economy,” Fouquet says, pointing to the 88 per cent jump in the company’s share price over the past year and its market value of €591bn.

He explains how investors that were enthused by Nvidia’s AI vision for chip design first realised how vital Taiwan’s TSMC was to the manufacture of those chips. “And then they started to wonder, ‘Oh, by the way, how does TSMC make those chips?’ And then they realised that they used this EUV machine [and] suddenly everyone realises there is only one company, ASML, making those machines.”

In a competitive global economy, how on earth did the world allow only one company in a small Dutch town to become another AI choke point to add to the squeezes on data centre construction and energy supply? “It’s complexity really,” Fouquet says, and I remember the jaw-dropping physics behind the $400mn EUV machine I had seen earlier in the day. The size of a double-decker bus, the machine prints circuits on to silicon wafers by firing 60,000 droplets of molten tin per second at them, using mirrors, lasers and short-wave light in a kind of vacuum-sealed nano-photocopier.

“Our customers were asking themselves . . . ‘If I only have one supplier, am I OK?’ . . . You could always say, ‘I’m going to get a second one’, but the amount of learning, the amount of investment and the amount of time you need to create that is huge.”

So trust is essential. “Our profit will grow with the [profits] of the industry, but we are not going to abuse the situation.” He admits “this is sometimes a difficult discussion” with shareholders: they might prefer the company to boost profit margins and put more debt on the balance sheet to accelerate investment and juice returns.

“We have that question every day . . . But it’s not about the money, that’s the beauty of it. If I could put a few billion down and get another 20 per cent capacity, I would do that. But because of the supply chain, it’s far more complex than that.”

ASML’s supply chain is something else. Where a typical industrial product might have a few dozen suppliers, an ASML EUV has more than 100,000 parts provided by 200 principal suppliers and 2,000 companies overall. That, Fouquet says, might limit the ability to increase production rapidly, but it has been key to the company’s performance, as the science has become ever more elaborate. “The more complex our products became . . . the more advantage we got in terms of competitiveness. We could [develop] a lot faster than anyone else.”

Rather than trying to make everything itself, ASML outsources to the best manufacturer of each component — Zeiss for optics, Trumpf for lasers, VDL for mechatronics. This has helped it crack problems that its competitors, notably Japanese groups Nikon and Canon, have failed to, leaving them focused only on previous-generation deep ultraviolet (DUV) technology. “We really needed the best brands across the world to get it done. I can tell you, if we had taken it upon ourselves . . . to do everything on EUV, there is no way we could have done it.”

On occasion, when suppliers have looked vulnerable, ASML has bought them to safeguard production. Laser maker Cymer, acquired in 2013, was one example. More recently ASML has taken an 11 per cent stake in French AI challenger Mistral. But collaboration normally trumps acquisition.

There is one big fly in the ointment: the US government. Itsban on exporting EUV technology to Chinablocks ASML from selling its most advanced, most profitable products to an AI market that is second only to the US. Although President Donald Trump has no direct jurisdiction over ASML (and is far less strict on Nvidia, which is allowed to sell its own EUV-made chips to China), the US has put pressure on the EU and on the Dutch government to impose an embargo on ASML — a source of clear frustration for the company.

“We understand that some technology may be restricted for obvious and legitimate concerns, but if we go too far, we are going to create the opposite results of what we’re trying to achieve in the first place,” says Fouquet. Namely, he says, China will be spurred to innovate itself —Huawei recently emergedas a pivotal force in China’s development of DUV machines, for example. “If you over-restrict, you bring desperation,” he goes on, no longer mild-mannered but exercised now. “And desperation creates a huge appetite for people to accelerate their own technology and, potentially, at some point, become strong competitors.” So is that his message to Trump?

“It’s not a message to Trump. It’s a message to all people who make those decisions,” he says bluntly. “I think the Dutch government decides for itself what it wants to export, or not, to China. So that’s first a message to the Dutch government [and] a message for the EU.”
We have yet to discuss the most clichéd question of all: whether AI — and thus the demand for the EUV machines and the other tech that underpins it — is a bubble ripe for bursting.

Fouquet admits the markets are jittery. But he insists this is no short-term sugar rush: the AI “revolution” will endure. “I think the AI effect on society and industry is going to take 10 to 15 years. We’re only seeing the tip of the iceberg.”
ASML is confident its EUV technology will evolve over a similar period. Transistor circuits will be stacked on top of each other. Mirror apertures will be increased to focus light more precisely.

Fouquet presents himself as an accidental CEO, a career semiconductor engineer who just grew with the industry. After studies in Grenoble and London, he worked in Israel and the US before landing at ASML 18 years ago and becoming the boss two years ago. (Having a physicist in charge again, after a financial manager, was a relief, confides one colleague.)

What tech is he most excited about now? “Humanoids will be among us . . . a few years from now,” he says. “We are just at the beginning of that cycle. [They] will be doing some of the tasks we all hate doing — the gardening, or emptying the dishwasher.” (He skates over my protest that many people love gardening.)

But what about truly transformative inventions? He is enthusiastic about the scope for “space tech” to revolutionise telecoms and energy production. But does he believe, for example, that nuclear fusion is finally within commercial reach? Are there lessons to learn from ASML’s success in developing a pioneering technology such as EUV after 20 years of trying? “For EUV”, Fouquet explains, “ASML thought the need would be absolutely there, therefore we put all our energy in it, almost at some point putting even the company at risk to get it done. I don’t think that you have that in some of those technologies [like fusion]. You need at some point people to believe that this is absolutely critical to get it done.” And rather than “200 people or 200 companies” pursuing the idea with splintered inefficiency, you need a monomania: “[You need] concentration when it comes to technology.”

After all this highbrow talk, I’m curious to know quite how the ASML boss reconciles running a company in the vanguard of the AI revolution with being a father to six children. Fouquet’s answer is refreshingly unscientific. “You could see the children as a burden,” he says. “But for me, it’s always made me stronger because the time I spend with my family, the time that I spend outside this office, is my rebalancing art . . . It gives me joy, and I think coming to work with joy is a lot better than not.”

title: Donald Trump hosts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at White House
paragraphs: Joe Millerin Washington andMichael Actonin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026

Donald Trump said he would dine with Anthropic chief Dario Amodei on Sunday evening, in a sign of rapprochement between the US president and the leader of the AI lab he has accused of being run by “leftwing nut jobs” and which his administration has labelled a national security risk.

The dinner at the White House, which Trump said would take place at 10pm, comes ahead of a meeting in Washington on Tuesday between the leaders of US AI companies and administration officials, amid a stand-off over AI regulation.

Amodei has beenleading the chargefor more stringent oversight of AI, calling for a slowdown in the release of frontier models, independent scrutiny of cyber security risks and increased co-ordination between labs and governments.

Trump has staked out the opposite position. The president has ruled out the establishment of a regulatory regime, warning it would slow the development of American AI — which he has called the “golden goose” — to the benefit of Chinese rivals.
Last week, he said the US “rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to controlAI.
“I’m for, let’s go and let’s win,” Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday. “We’re about a year, maybe a year and a half, up on China. There is nobody in third place.”
Donald Trump says he will talk to Anthropic chief Dario Amodei about AI at the White House
In comments to the media ahead of the planned dinner, Trump called Amodei “very highly respected”. Anthropic declined to comment.
Concern is also growing over AI agents going rogue. On Friday, OpenAI said it had notified “dozens” of partners, including governments, that its tools hadbreached their systems.
That followed news last week that an OpenAI agent hadhacked an Australianpublic health service website, accessing public and non-public files.
AI research group Transluce last week said the latest incidents appeared to involve agents trawling the internet for information during repeated training exercises and going off-script.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI’s models were involved in a high-profile breach of AI model platform Hugging Face in July during security testing.
OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk have joined Amodei in calling for a “pacing” of AI development so that safety testing can keep up with the technology’s deployment.
Musk is set to visit Washington for Tuesday’s event, alongside Nvidia’s Jensen Huang — who hasdismissed callsfor laws to govern AI — and other Anthropic officials.

Amodei’s meeting with Trump comes after a federal appeals court in Washington last week kept in place a Pentagon ban on Anthropic’s products, which was imposed this year after the company included restrictions on the use of its AI in warfare.
Defence secretary Pete Hegseth at the time accused Amodei of putting on a “masterclass in arrogance”, while Trump denounced the company as “radical left”.
A separate court in California ruled in August that the Pentagon had engaged in “unlawful retaliation”. Anthropic is exploring a further appeal of the Washington decision.
Additional reporting by Amy Mackinnon in Washington

title: Why everyone's a creator - even the CEO | FT Working It
paragraphs: Everyone needs a personal brand - from the company’s newest intern, to the most established CEO, and in the AI era the rules of engagement are changing fast. In the second in a series of films, FT Working It editor Isabel Berwick explains how to harness the power of a personal brand.
You can enable subtitles (captions) in the video player

Everyone needs a personal brand across global industries, from the company's newest intern to the most established CEO. Until recently, winning over fans was the work of famous actors and sports stars. Today, just about anyone can become well-known as a content creator.
So anyone with a phone and a point of view can pick it up and create content, and potentially reach an audience of millions.
We're talking hundreds of millions of people potentially in this market right now.
In the AI era, the rules are changing fast.

The thing about business development is you're so desperate to have a topic to talk to somebody about. And it's those opening seconds. If you can find any sort of a coat hook to continue that chat on, that's good for the business.

I'm Isabel Berwick. I lead the FT's Working It brand, speaking, presenting and writing about management, leadership and workplaces. In this series, I'll explore some of the most pressing issues around the future of work, and talk to senior leaders about how they are making work better.
Trust is a real big part of it, and that's what we're really trying to build.

If the corporate ladder is broken, and even if it isn't, there are a huge range of jobs that didn't exist even a few years ago. Content creation, branding, side hustles. Relying on an employer is not going to work in an uncertain future. People trust people in a world where institutions are now treated with suspicion.

The Edelman Trust Barometer finds that the public trusts individuals over institutions. That presents an opportunity for people to build their brands, whether that's inside or outside a corporate workplace. I travelled to Dublin to interview William Peake, the global managing partner of international law firm Harneys. William posts often and honestly on LinkedIn, a strategy that helps him set the strategic and cultural agenda for his global offshore law firm.
How did you get into making short videos, posting? Because the law is quite a staid place.

I could see that there was a real opportunity there on LinkedIn. And I could see that nobody was actually sharing any real version of themselves, hugely curated content from law firms. Totally artificial and not real. And I thought, there's an opportunity here. And I've always known how to write an engaging hook. So I started with posting and then I drifted into video content. Because clearly, that was getting really good traction on the platform.
What sort of topics do you post about?

I post about things that are on my desk, and I think that's the bit that connects with people. So I'm not posting around pro forma topics. I'm posting around things that people can say, oh, that's actually an issue that we're dealing with. I talk a lot about the challenges of leadership. I talk about the journey for junior lawyers, the advice that they need that I wish I had received.

That authenticity and behind-the-scenes access helps to engage digital audiences. And like it or not, from corporates to creatives, broadcasting a professional identity is something many more of us need to do, according to experts. I asked Mary Bekhait, chief executive of YMU, a management company representing talent in sport, music, and entertainment, about the changing media landscape.

So historically, our talent, if they wanted to reach a mass audience, they needed to go through a gatekeeper. That might be a broadcaster, that might be a record label or a publisher. And now, social media has changed all of that. So anyone with a phone and a point of view can pick it up and create content and potentially reach an audience of millions.

And that's completely changed the game in terms of talent, but also where power resides. Because historically, power resides with the people that distributed the content. Now, power resides with the individuals that own the audience. And we're seeing the most sophisticated creators build really significant businesses off the back of that.
And I guess this plays into both the individual creator economy and the corporate brand economy, that we trust people more than we trust institutions.
Why do you think that's happening? And where do you see that going?

I think trust is becoming more personal, generally. I think we're so bombarded with information and advertising and AI-generated content that it's actually really difficult to navigate this incredibly complex landscape. I wake up and I open the phone and it's like a million messages instantly at once. I think people naturally gravitate towards those individuals that can hold their hand through that, and where they believe what they believe, and they feel that there's actually been a relationship built over time.

So I think showing up consistently has really helped creators build enormous levels of trust. Because trust is hard to build and it's easy to lose. But I think in this AI kind of flooded world, trust is actually the scarce commodity.
Building trust goes hand-in-hand with creating community.
Frankie, tell us who you are and what you do.

So I'm Frankie Bridge, and I run a business called Faves The Edit. And it's an online community, mainly on Instagram, but we have a subscribed mailer that goes out every week. And what we do is we curate and edit our favourite pieces from the high street to take out the stress for busy women trying to look for pieces or trying to come up with ideas of what to wear if they're feeling stuck.

But we also now do live events. So we do live runways during Fashion Week. We are trying to build a community for women who want to meet like-minded people, and maybe feel like they haven't been welcomed into the fashion space previously. And we're trying to break down those barriers and make everyone feel welcome.
Amazing pieces. And they were completely sold out.
So how did it start? Because you've had a long career. You were a star at 12 or 13 when you were in bands. How have you got from there to here?

Well, I mean, it's been a long time. I think for me, performing was always such a passion of mine from such a young age, clearly, starting work. Ended up in a band, S Club Juniors at the age of 12, then another pop group called The Saturdays as I got a bit older. And I think it's really difficult when you have already achieved your passion at such a young age.
So what's the difference between having engaged followers on Instagram, for example, and building a community? What's your advice to other people?

I think there's such a big difference. I think community at the moment is a real buzzword. I think brands have realised that community is needed. And it's definitely true. I think we have become such an online world, especially since Covid and things like that. And it has so many benefits. But also, I think it's made people feel isolated and disconnected. And people are trying to create more in-real-life experiences.

So in this film we're also talking about personal brand. In a corporate job, actually, how that's becoming... the creator economy has moved into the corporate sphere. What would be your advice to somebody who's in 9 to 5 corporate job who wants to build a little bit of a brand?

I think it's really hard for a lot of business people. People in corporate, I feel like they've always been the person that would never be in front of the camera. And now, as an economy, we are asking people to be the face of these things because we who they are. And like we keep saying, to have that connection, I think it can feel really unnatural and really embarrassing for some reason.

But I think that comes from feeling judged by other people and stepping outside of your comfort zone. I have friends who have recently started businesses who have never used social media for their work. And they're constantly saying to me, oh, I can't post this because it's cringey or it's embarrassing. And I'm like, but to who? At first, people might judge you, or at first people might say something.

But when you're successful, no one's going to judge you anymore. Everyone will just accept it. So I would say you have to push past that embarrassment factor and also act like you already have a million followers. I think we have this embarrassment, oh, I've only got 500 followers or whatever. But everyone has to start somewhere. And I always say, there's still 500 people that have taken the time to engage with you. And that will only grow.
Behind-the-scenes authenticity helps creatives and corporates to build online presence. Those skills are transcending boundaries and sectors.

The internet has created this huge economy now where people can say what they want to say whenever they want to say it. As long as they've got a smartphone and they've got a platform, which YouTube is one of them, TikTok, X to some degree. And this changes the whole dynamics of media, right? Because suddenly, those traditional gatekeepers of what goes out there, they don't really exist anymore.

They've got audiences, clearly. But they have to now follow what the creators are doing. title: Kremlin pressures Russian businesses to pay for drone defences
paragraphs: Anastasia StogneiandMax Seddonin Berlin,Katya Areninain Vilnius
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Vladimir Putin is shifting the burden of anti-drone defences on to businesses, with companies that fail to protect their assets from Ukrainian strikes now facing the prospect of state takeover.

The move is part of the Kremlin’s response to Kyiv’s intensifying long-range drone campaign that set dozens of commercial warehouses on fire and destroyed as much as 20 per cent ofRussia’s refining capacity, leaving the petrostate scrambling for fuel.

In late August, the Russian president signed a decree allowing the introduction of “temporary management” at “critical infrastructure objects” that fail to protect themselves against drones. Three days later, the government established a committee to oversee implementation.

A former Kremlin official told the FT thatPutinsigned the decree after his intelligence services and the military sought to shift responsibility for drone defence on to companies. “They complained that businesses were sitting on their hands and don’t want to lift a finger, and Putin agreed,” the person said. “The message is: guys, get your act together and start spending,” he added.
Vyacheslav Plaksin, a drone defence expert, said inquiries from businesses increased fivefold almost overnight after the decree was issued. “The decree served as a trigger,” he said.
Putin appeared satisfied with the result. “Companies have got involved and started putting money in,” he said on September 3.

Throughout the full-scale war in Ukraine, businesses and the state have wrangled over who should foot the bill. The frustration reached such a high level that even Alexander Shokhin, the head of Russia’s Kremlin-loyal business lobby group, has repeatedly urged the state to help businesses finance the defence project.

But the government was adamant. “They [the businesses] have the money,” finance minister Anton Siluanov said at Russia’s flagship economic forum in June. In late September, the finance ministry finally said it was preparing “tax changes” to recognise companies’ spending on defence, though no details were disclosed.

Putin’s decree ended the debate and fuelled fears among businesses that the Kremlin could use the new powers as another route to nationalisation. State seizures have become increasingly common since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including of assets formerly owned by western companies. Recent cases include the de facto seizure of Auchan and Nestlé subsidiaries.
Putin insisted that he had “never even considered taking anything away” with the decree, but the assurance did little to dispel concerns among business figures.

“Undoubtedly, it will be used to snap up assets at some point,” said a former executive of Rosneft, Russia’s state-backed oil company. But for now, it is a way to force business owners to “make people stump up”.

Some companies with close ties to the Kremlin, including Rosneft, could even benefit from the arrangement, the person added. “They will be able to offload their refineries on to the state temporarily, have them patched up [at public expense] and take them back when better times return,” he explained.

There are still no clear rules on who is responsible for protecting facilities from Ukrainian drone strikes or what measures they are required to take. Many anti-drone defences require hard-to-obtain permits. Putin’s decree introduced penalties without clarifying the underlying rules.
“Legislation is now like a jigsaw puzzle that every company has to put together itself,” said Plaksin.
Russia’s anti-drone rules have evolved from older anti-terrorism regulations, leaving companies to navigate dozens of overlapping requirements, from electronic warfare systems to protective netting.

Hundreds of thousands of companies could fall within the rules. Plaksin said that, in one industry alone, officials discussed prioritising 24,000 critical sites out of about 700,000 in total. The list, the government said, would remain secret.

Businesses sought urgent clarification on whether they fell under the new requirements. Shopping mall operators were told they were “unlikely to be included at this stage” and could “decide for themselves”, a person familiar with the situation told the FT.

Although Russia is trying to keep such measures under wraps, satellite imagery reveals some of what has been put in place.

“At vulnerable sites such as military airfields, oil refineries and power plants, we can frequently see anti-drone netting and reinforced concrete structures shielding critical assets,” said a former Ukrainian officer who operates the analytical group Frontelligence Insight. Air-defence systems such as Pantsir can also be positioned nearby, including in residential areas.

The closer a critical facility is to Ukraine, the more sophisticated its defences tend to be, the person said. “A power plant in Crimea may implement nearly all of the protective measures described above,” while infrastructure “beyond the Ural Mountains may have only limited protection, or in some cases none at all.”

Drone defence ranges from passive measures such as netting to electronic warfare. But almost anything involving the destruction or jamming of drones requires permits from the security services, which most companies — apart from a handful of energy and financial heavyweights — do not have.

Reservists — civilians who remain in regular jobs while contracted to the military reserve — can be used by companies for protection, but are not allowed to carry weapons, the former Rosneft executive said. That means companies need separate arrangements with the military and National Guard.

“Every big company strikes deals with nearby military units. Some of them are now entirely tied up guarding a particular factory instead of performing their regular duties,” he said. A powerful Pantsir air-defence system can be deployed to a company site only at the defence ministry’s initiative and remains under military control.
But even basic anti-drone defences available on the open market carry a hefty price tag.

The cost to individual companies varies depending on their size and the requirements imposed on them. Plaksin cited one factory that needed to install a protection system costing Rbs220mn ($2.8mn) — equivalent to one day’s revenue.

A businessman in a region bordering Ukraine that is under frequent attack told the FT he had spent more than Rbs1.5bn ($19.1mn) on air defences. At an economic forum earlier in September, Putin mentioned an oil company spending “dozens of billions of roubles” on anti-drone defences.

“The state does not have money both to keep fighting the war and to build a layered defence against drones,” said Alexandra Prokopenko, a fellow at Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center. “And businesses have nowhere to turn.”
According to the former Rosneft executive, “this has become yet another new tax”.

But the government was adamant. “They [the businesses] have the money,” finance minister Anton Siluanov said at Russia’s flagship economic forum in June. In late September, the finance ministry finally said it was preparing “tax changes” to recognise companies’ spending on defence, though no details were disclosed.

Putin’s decree ended the debate and fuelled fears among businesses that the Kremlin could use the new powers as another route to nationalisation. State seizures have become increasingly common since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including of assets formerly owned by western companies. There are still no clear rules on who is responsible for protecting facilities from Ukrainian drone strikes or what measures they are required to take. Many anti-drone defences require hard-to-obtain permits. Putin’s decree introduced penalties without clarifying the underlying rules.

“Legislation is now like a jigsaw puzzle that every company has to put together itself,” said Plaksin.

Russia’s anti-drone rules have evolved from older anti-terrorism regulations, leaving companies to navigate dozens of overlapping requirements, from electronic warfare systems to protective netting.

Hundreds of thousands of companies could fall within the rules. Plaksin said that, in one industry alone, officials discussed prioritising 24,000 critical sites out of about 700,000 in total. The list, the government said, would remain secret.

Businesses sought urgent clarification on whether they fell under the new requirements. Shopping mall operators were told they were “unlikely to be included at this stage” and could “decide for themselves”, a person familiar with the situation told the FT.

Although Russia is trying to keep such measures under wraps, satellite imagery reveals some of what has been put in place.

title: Netanyahu under pressure over reports he was warned about October 7
paragraphs: James Shotterin Jerusalem,Neri Zilberin Tel Aviv andAndrew Englandin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026

Benjamin Netanyahu was facing a growing backlash from his political opponents on Monday following reports that Egyptian and Emirati officials had warned the Israeli prime minister that Hamas was preparing an attack on Israel before its October 7 2023 assault.

The leaks, which follow reported warnings to Israel that emerged in 2023 and 2024, come a month before what is expected to be a knife-edge election in Israel. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is trailing a diverse group of opposition parties in the polls, although both blocs remain short of a majority.

Yair Golan, head of the leftwing Democrats, posted a video of Netanyahu talking in June 2023 about the threat of Hamas attacking Israel, adding: “You knew. You ignored it. Netanyahu, you’re the one in charge. You’re responsible.”

His criticism was echoed by Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister under Netanyahu who leads the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party, who said he had warned the prime minister as early as 2016 of the risk of a cross-border attack by Hamas.

Netanyahu has denied receiving prior warning of Hamas’s attack, which is widely regarded as the worst security failure in Israel’s history, and sought to pin the blame for the debacle on the country’s military and intelligence services.

Haaretz reported earlier this month that the UAE’s leader, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, had spoken to Netanyahu just a week and a half before October 7 and warned him that Hamas’s leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major operation against Israel.

Netanyahu denied the report and threatened to sue Haaretz for libel over the story. He also denied he had been warned of an attack by Abbas Kamel, the then head of Egyptian intelligence, and said that he had ordered a libel suit to be filed “on this matter as well” following a report in the Wall Street Journal that Kamel had called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to deliver such a warning.
On Sunday, Netanyahu flew to the UAE — Israel’s closest Arab ally — for an unannounced meeting with Sheikh Mohamed.

The UAE’s state news agency said on Monday that the two leaders discussed bilateral relations and ways to strengthen them — in the first official acknowledgment of any visit to the Gulf state by the Israeli prime minister.

Israeli media reported that Netanyahu had asked Sheikh Mohamed to deny passing him a warning. Two people briefed on the meeting confirmed that the Haaretz article had been discussed but did not confirm whether Netanyahu had requested a denial.
The Israeli prime minister’s office said the suggestion Netanyahu asked for a denial was “fake news”. The Emirati foreign ministry declined to comment.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, which is the biggest in most opinion polls, said on Sunday that Netanyahu had “clearly and unequivocally betrayed the public’s trust and his duty”.

“Netanyahu blindly, complacently and irresponsibly led the state of Israel into the greatest disaster in its history,” Eisenkot said during a public gathering of families of victims of October 7 in Tel Aviv, in comments broadcast by Israeli media.
An Arab diplomat said the leaks reported in the press were an indication that “many in the region don’t want Netanyahu to win the election”.

Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political analyst, said the scope for the leaks to persuade voters to change their minds on Netanyahu was limited. There had been multiple reports over the past three years about the failures that preceded Hamas’s attack, and most voters had already made up their minds on Netanyahu, she added.

“It has been three years, and people know what they think about Netanyahu,” Scheindlin said. “All the people who are against him are already furious over October 7. And people on his side have a very clear narrative of what happened, and that it is all the responsibility of the security services.”
Egypt’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Additional reporting by Chloe Cornish in Dubai and Heba Saleh in Cairo

title: HSBC moves to bolster Hang Seng by cleaning up balance sheet
paragraphs: Arjun Neil Alimin Hong Kong
PublishedSeptember 28 2026

HSBC moved HK$11bn of loans off Hang Seng’s balance sheet in the first half of the year in the clearest sign yet that Europe’s largest lender is moving to clean up the Hong Kong bank it now fully controls.
Hang Seng sold a loan portfolio for HK$11bn ($1.4bn) to HSBC’s Asia-Pacific subsidiary on “arm’s-length terms”, according to a related-party transaction disclosure it made in August.

The disclosures did not specify whether the loans were “non-performing” or distressed, but in the first six months of the year Hang Seng’s “stage 3” impaired loans fell by HK$20bn ($2.6bn) to HK$37bn.
A significant proportion ofHSBC’s bad loans in Hong Kong are concentrated in Hang Seng, making the lender appear weaker and less profitable, leading to reduced lending.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Hang Seng’s non-performing loan ratio stood at a record 7 per cent in December 2025, above the heights of the Asian financial crisis. By the end of June this year the ratio had fallen to 4.6 per cent, indicating a rapid turnaround.

Its allowances for expected credit losses decreased by HK$1.6bn to HK$17.5bn even as the bank took an expected credit loss (ECL) charge of HK$2.4bn for the first half of 2026. That was about half the amount it took in the same period last year.
HSBC declined to comment on the deal, but executives have previously spoken about improving the capital efficiency of Hang Seng — which implies less impaired debt on its balance sheet.
“We have started focusing much more on how we will drive capital efficiency through balance sheet velocity,” said outgoing chief financial officer Pam Kaur on a call with analysts earlier this month.

“This includes how we are allocating our business across different legal entities, for example by adjusting the mix of portfolios between Hang Seng and HSBC in Hong Kong, so that everybody can participate in those growth opportunities with the right risk returns and levels of NPLs [non-performing loans], and as a result, the right degree of capital efficiency,” Kaur said.

Hong Kong’s real estate market struggled to recover after the pandemic, suffering several years of falling rents and rising vacancy rates. The slump hit the territory’s property developers, many of which hold loans from Hang Seng.
The move comes after the FT reported in July that HSBC was seeking buyers forrisky Hang Seng loansfollowing its takeover of the local bank.
HSBC has also taken other steps since it took full control of Hang Seng. Over the summer the bank combined many back-office executive roles between its Hong Kong organisation and Hang Seng.
“The privatisation of Hang Seng enables us to scale capabilities and drive growth for all our existing and new customers,” said HSBC in reference to the leadership changes.

“The new leaders will explore opportunities for greater collaboration and alignment in support of the differentiated propositions. We are focused on delivering the best of HSBC and Hang Seng to our customers more efficiently.”

HSBC has also scrapped certain benefits for its bankers, including asubsidy to join private members’ clubs, in an attempt to harmonise benefits between staff from the London-based lender and Hang Seng employees.
HSBC first bought a controlling stake in Hang Seng, a local retail bank with a strong brand, during a financial crisis in 1965.

The deal turned Hang Seng into a dominant local participant and ranks among HSBC’s most strategically significant transactions. Last year, the London-headquartered bank said it would buy out minority investors totake Hang Seng private for $13.6bn.
At the time, HSBC chief executive Georges Elhedery denied that the decision was sparked by concerns over Hang Seng’s commercial property exposure.

title: ‘No definitive timeline’ for David Solomon to step down as CEO, says Goldman Sachs
paragraphs: Joshua Franklinin New York
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
Goldman Sachs said there was “no definitive timeline” for chief executive David Solomon to step down following a report that his deputy John Waldron could succeed him as early as next year.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday that Goldman’s board had discussed Waldron taking over towards the end of 2027 or in 2028. The newspaper also said that Solomon could become executive chair for a year or two after that.

Goldmanspokesperson Tony Fratto said: “Of course the board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings, but there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs. Any assertions about timing are just speculation.”
Waldron, Goldman’s president and chief operating officer, iswidely seenas the heir apparent to Solomon, who has run the investment bank since 2018 when he replaced Lloyd Blankfein.
Both Solomon and Waldron were granted five-year retention bonuses, worth $80mn apiece, at the start of 2025. Solomon does not need to remain as chief executive during that time to earn the payout.

Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said in a note that Waldron was “close to David Solomon, already carries broad responsibilities, received a major retention award, sits on the board and is well known internally and externally. The bigger question is what happens to other senior executives who are passed over for president or COO.”

Waldron has knownSolomonsince the early 1990s when he started his Wall Street career at Bear Stearns. Solomon later recruited Waldron to Goldman in 2000 and the two have risen in tandem. Solomon appointed Waldron as president when he became chief executive eight years ago.
The first half of Solomon’s tenure running Goldman was blighted by a lossmaking expansion in retail banking — a Main Street push that was at odds with the investment bank’s Wall Street pedigree.

After billions of dollars in losses, Solomon largely exited the consumer push and has doubled down on investment banking, trading and money management. The bank’s stock is up about 180 per cent in the past three years.

Waldron had been approached by private capital firm Apollo Global in 2024 but ultimately stayed at Goldman, which rewarded him with a seat on Goldman’s board and retention bonuses. These moves have highlighted the view that Waldron was Solomon’s planned successor.

title: Why Europe’s centre will hold
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026

Last Chance: The New Chancellor and the Struggle for Democracyby Robin Alexander was a bestselling book in Germany last year. It captured a widespread fear that, if Chancellor Friedrich Merz fails, the political extremes could overwhelm German democracy.

A year on, those concerns are rising. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), a far-right populist party, has topped the polls in two recent state elections — while the far-left Die Linke has just won the Berlin state election. Merz’s popularity rating hasplummetedto 13 per cent. There is widespread speculation that he may soon have to resign.

Germany is Europe’s largest economy, so whatever happens there will shake the whole continent. Meanwhile, in France, the EU’s second-largest economy, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the far-right Rassemblement National, leads the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election.
So is Europe’s centre about to crumble? And is European democracy really squandering its “last chance”?
Fortunately, political reality is rather less dramatic. Despite all the current turmoil, Europe’s political centre is likely to hold.

There are three main reasons for this. The first is the widespread use of proportional representation in European elections. The second is the tendency of far-right parties to either fail or moderate in government. That reflects a third point — the serious constraints that membership of the EU places on populist, anti-establishment parties.
Parties that are widely regarded as “far right” have already entered government in important European countries. The results were instructive.

In the Netherlands, the PVV led by Geert Wilders emerged from elections in 2023 as the single largest party and briefly anchored a coalition government. But, eventually, the Wilders party became frustrated by the constraints of coalition politics and EU law and stalked out of government. The PVV’s support fell sharply at the next election — and the Netherlands is currently governed by another centrist coalition.

Austria’s far-right Freedom Party has also been part of two coalition governments since 2000 — and won the most votes in the 2024 elections. But it has been unable to form a coalition government and is currently out of power.

The Dutch and Austrian experiences underline how proportional representation limits the political options of the far right. That is particularly relevant in Germany, where centrist parties have a “firewall” policy that prohibits going into office with the far right.

The AfD is currently polling just below 30 per cent at a national level. If it hits those levels in a national election, or even goes above them, it would be much harder to form a centrist coalition. But the chances are that the AfD would still be locked out of power.
The situation in France is different because the second round of the presidential election is a winner-takes-all contest. If Le Pen is victorious next May, then she will enter the Élysée Palace.

But the example of Italy suggests that a far-right government in France might not be as extreme as some fear. Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, leads a political party that has its origins in the Mussolini-admiring far right. But she has largely governed from the centre right — avoiding a confrontation with her EU partners that might have cost EU funds and spooked the debt markets.

The Italian left points to Meloni’s harsher policies on immigration and asylum as indications that she retains far-right instincts. But almost all European governments are now searching for ways to limit the flow of asylum seekers. This is a response to growing voter unease — so arguably an expression of democracy rather than its negation.

Le Pen has been moderating her party’s image for many years — shedding many of its more extreme policies and associations. In the process, she has broken with her own father, the founder of the party, and ditched plans to leave the European single currency.

The far-right leader still retains instincts that differ sharply from the French mainstream. She recently pledged to end all French financial aid to Ukraine. Some of her policies — such as a pledge for national preference for French jobseekers and businesses — would put her at odds with EU law.

But, once in office, Le Pen is likely to find that a full-scale confrontation with the rest of the EU would come at too high a political and economic cost. Membership of a functioning EU internal market remains key to the health of the French economy. The country’s voters know this. The bond markets — which are another big constraint on the indebted French and Italian governments — would also take fright.

Many of the fears around Le Pen, the AfD and the rest of the European far right reflect the memories of the 1930s. The experience then was that once far-right leaders — such as Hitler or Franco — took power, they swiftly undermined democracy and only left office when they died.

But contemporary Europe’s experience has been very different. The far right has entered government — and then left it peacefully. Even Hungary’s Viktor Orbán accepted defeat in an election earlier this year.
The rise of the AfD and Le Pen is dramatic and will increase political tensions and instability. But it does not spell the end of European democracy.

Such outsize demand has created credit markets that can support larger and longer-term debt issues than ever before. But it has distorted pricing, with highly rated bonds sometimes trading at discounts to lesser-quality issues because of the sudden glut in supply.

Analogies with the bust that followed the railway boom of the 19th century, which was also capital-intensive and largely debt-financed, are commonplace.

In the wake of mounting worries by equity investors that the world’s stock markets are dangerously tied to the fortunes of AI, the same risk is creeping into the bond market — risking an even bigger fallout if cracks emerge.

title: Why investors think Panama will overcome Trump threats
paragraphs: Christine Murrayin Mexico City andJoseph Cotterillin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Foreign investors have been buying up Panama’s debt, betting that the Central American country can stage a remarkable recovery from a recent political and social crisis that threatened to badly damage its economy.

Despitemass proteststhat closed its largest foreign investment — a copper mine accounting for 5 per cent of GDP — and deterred other investors, followed by a threat by US President Donald Trump last year to “take back” the Panama Canal, Panama’s bonds have performed much better than many investors had expected.
The premium over US Treasuries it pays to borrow has dropped from as much as 3.5 percentage points in 2023 and 2024 to about 1.5 percentage points, in a sign of demand for the bonds.
Finance minister Felipe Chapman told the FT that, while it would take time for some policies to take effect, the government’s fiscal restraint had helped lure back investors.
“You have to first put the house in order, physically speaking, then you have to reconstruct or rebuild confidence and trust,” he said.

“The last time we went to the global market was in February and I was personally expecting a premium of about 160 [basis points, or 1.6 percentage points], now we closed at about 145,” he said. “So it was awesome, we’re very happy.”

Panama’s long-dated dollar bonds currently trade at yields of 6 to 6.5 per cent, below the bonds of higher-rated US AI companies such as Meta, although countries such as Chile, Guatemala and Peru have smaller risk premiums over Treasuries.

Its economy has accelerated this year after a sharp slowdown, growing 6.4 per cent year on year in the second quarter after 4.8 per cent in the first quarter, ranking it as one of the fastest-growing in the region. A wide range of sectors have shared in the growth, including construction and tourism, as well as more activity around the country’s canal after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“A few quarters ago a sort of abyss was at the nation’s doorstep,” said UBS analyst Alberto Rojas in a recent note. “That is no longer the case; now the good times are starting to roll in.”

For decades, Panama was considered the poster child of Latin America among investors, with high growth, relatively solid institutions and a business-friendly environment. In 2018, it became a high-income economy under World Bank definitions, joining a small club of just three other nations in Latin America, with aspirations to become the “Singapore of Latin America” as a prosperous finance and trading hub.

But social discontent over government corruption and huge inequality exploded into protests in 2023 thatshut down the copper mine, which is owned by Canada’s First Quantum and which had been expected to add billions of dollars in royalties to the country’s coffers and boost economic growth. title: The bargain between shareholders and companies is being eroded
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
The writer is chief executive of Norges Bank Investment Management
When you buy a share in a company, you enter into a bargain. You take the price as it comes, up or down, and in return you get a set of rights.
These include a vote on the decisions that matter, reliable information about the company, a fair share of the value created and a way to enforce the rights if they are denied.

Well, at least this is how it used to be. This bargain is now being rewritten. Not in one market but in many, across Asia, Europe and the Americas. Some 60 per cent of jurisdictions around the world now allow shares with unequal voting powers, up from 44 per cent in 2020, according to OECD figures from last year. And in the US, 36 per cent of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares, the highest share recorded since the Council of Institutional Investors began tracking this in 2017.

As a long term-investor and owner of shares in more than 7,000 companies around the world, these developments worry us greatly. Why do we care so much? Because strong shareholder rights are profitable, not only for us but for the market as a whole.

Research indicates that strong shareholder rights go with deeper, more liquid markets and broader access to financing. Weakening them raises the cost of capital, and companies with stronger protections have historically traded at higher valuations.

Rights also create trust, and trust is what keeps long-term money invested when short-term money heads for the exit. We own a piece of almost every listed company across markets, and we cannot simply sell out. If those companies succeed, so do we. We share this interest with everyone who depends on healthy markets — savers, pensioners and businesses that need capital to grow.

What is it that worries us? First of all, the vote is being diluted. More companies are listing with two share classes so that the largest owners can retain control. Such structures can attract founders to go public, which is something we encourage. However, over time each share should carry equal say.

Second, reporting requirements are under pressure in several markets. Shareholders cannot see inside a company or tell whether it is run in their interest. They depend on what companies disclose. The limiting of any reporting cost that serves no one is something we welcome (andhave argued forin the past), but removing public information that shareholders rely on is not.

Third, shareholders have a right to a share of any payout in proportion to what they own. They should be protected from transactions that move value to a controlling shareholder or to management at their expense. But safeguards against such transactions are being weakened in several markets, leaving shareholders with fewer ways to identify and challenge them.

And finally, we see that access to the courts is narrowing. A right is only as good as the means to enforce it. Shareholders should be able to choose where to bring a claim and pursue it without excessive cost or delay. Safeguards against meaningless lawsuits are reasonable but safeguards that also block claims with merit and weaken protection for all shareholders are not.
Each of these changes may appear reasonable on its own, but together they represent a concerning weakening of shareholder rights.

We want more companies to come to the market, not fewer. So, we believe that listing should not be made needlessly burdensome. But there is a trade-off. Competition between financial centres should not turn into competition to offer investors the least.

We love speed and we love a great race. But not one that could easily turn out to be a race to the bottom. Everyone in the market has a role and an interest in protecting these rights. But no one can protect these rights alone.

Regulators should keep their frameworks steady, which is itself a form of investor protection. Exchanges should hold the governance line they set, even when competition for listings pushes the other way. Index providers should give governance real weight in their inclusion rules, which now decide what many investors end up owning. Boards should protect shareholder rights through the governance choices they make, including where to incorporate and list. Finally, investors should use their own rights and back the efforts to defend them.
The bargain on buying shares was built on the back of strong shareholder rights. It will not hold together unless we all step up.

Good morning. So far, a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.2 per cent doesn’t bother US stocks. The S&P 500 rose Friday and remains right in the trading range it has been in since the beginning of August, when the yield was 4.6 per cent. That economic growth is a major driver of the yield increase certainly helps. The big risk, as we described on thepodcastlast week, is that the rapid rise in yields causes some sort of financial accident. But maybe we’ll get lucky!
Usually we run interviews on Fridays but the bond market excitement disrupted our plans. Email us:[email protected].

Helen Thompson is professor of political economy at the University of Cambridge and the author ofDisorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century. Her work focuses on energy, geopolitics and the economic pressures reshaping western democracies. She spoke toUnhedgedearlier this month about the latest energy shock, China and US energy power, high debt levels and the politics of central bank independence. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Unhedged:During the post-pandemic inflation surge, people reached for historical analogies to understand that moment. What analogies explain the current energy shock?

Helen Thompson:In the 2021-22 energy shock there were some parallels with the 1970s. In both periods western countries had become accustomed to relatively low oil prices and experienced considerable domestic problems that arose not just from the high energy prices but also from the geopolitical conditions that caused it.

But the parallel that should have been drawn was to the oil price shock from 2005-08, which I think is underestimated in the history of the past couple of decades. A great deal of that was China’s demand for oil. Likewise, the beginning of the gas shock in 2021-22 wasn’t Russia’s invasion of Ukraine but China’s demand for liquefied natural gas which surged in the autumn of 2021. So actually the parallel is one of western countries having to adjust to China’s energy demand, which they haven’t been very good at over this century.
Unhedged:What makes the latest energy shock structural rather than temporary?

Thompson:From the late 1970s the US took responsibility for guaranteeing maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and out into the Persian Gulf. While the US had problems projecting military power in the Middle East, it has not had a problem acting as that guarantor. Now we’re seeing the US willing to accept turmoil around transit through the Gulf for months on end and, to some extent, being part of the reason why, given the blockade it imposed on some ships coming out of the Gulf.

I don’t think we’re ever really going back to a world in which the US acting as a guarantor of passage through the Strait of Hormuz can be taken for granted. And you can see that in the way in which various Arab states, including Saudi Arabia, are working on the presumption that they need pipelines. You are going to see Arab states really trying to move as far away as they can from reliance on maritime passage through that body of water.
Unhedged:Why has the global economy proved more resilient to the oil shock than expected?

Thompson:First, I think a large part of it is China’s demand destruction. China, in some sense, did prepare, if not exactly for this war, then for a similar war, given the amount of oil stockpiling that it did. The Chinese leadership have a quite good understanding of the geopolitical risks around their energy security and have taken that a lot more seriously than European countries have.

Second, the drawdowns from the US shouldn’t be underestimated in the explanation. But something that has surprised me is the ability of US producers to supply European countries with refined petroleum products. I think it suggests there’s more flexibility in the shale industry than might have been expected.
Unhedged:Many of the advanced economies are facing extraordinary debt levels and high borrowing costs. Do you think this will lead to financial repression?

Thompson:I think that’s been the direction of travel for some time. In a way, quantitative easing is a form of financial repression. It’s obviously very different from trying to directly cap yields but you’re still using the power of the central bank to support debt and keep yields low. QE has gone away but the need to sustain high levels of debt hasn’t gone away and in some cases it has got worse. So you are going to have something to replace what QE was doing.

The more formal ways of doing financial repression are just harder than they were before. They run into the hard constraints that international capital flows have imposed on the world economy since the 1970s — 1980s. We’re in quite uncertain territory because the ways in which the problem [of high debt levels] has been dealt with in the past are not really workable any longer. So I think we’re going to see lots of improvisation to achieve the same ends, which is sort of what Bessent has been trying to do.
Unhedged:Do you see any overall coherence to the Trump administration’s economic policy?

Thompson:I think that there is actually more rationality than there may seem. What I think is clear in the US, and what you can see in [Stephen Miran’s]Mar-a-Lago accordpaper, that for some of the people who have been economic advisers to Trump is the idea that US has a fundamental debt problem, the trajectory of the debt is unsustainable, and one of the reasons it’s unsustainable is because the interest on it is too high. I think we can see that they want to make the US debt more sustainable by paying less interest on it. And they will try to go about that through different means, some more strategic, some tactical. Whether that can succeed is a whole other question.
Unhedged:Is the 1990s conception of central bank independence still suited to the current political and economic challenges?
Thompson:It seems to me that you get a change in what the relationship is between politics and monetary policy at different economic and political junctures.

Central banks like the BoE were given independence against a relatively benign international monetary background. If you told them to keep inflation to 2 per cent or lower, that was both doable and didn’t come with hard trade-offs. I think that era ended with the crash. And, actually, we did get a political version of monetary policy. It just didn’t look how it had looked in the past because it was QE. But once QE has become so hard, what do you do now? I don’t think anybody really knows the answer. But I think [political monetary policy] is what you would expect once you’ve gone back to an underlying international monetary and financial order that is much less benign than the one that prevailed when the BoE was given its independence.

There’s almost a kind of “end of history” — type argument around the BoE’s independence. It was somehow the liberal thing to do. It’s what competent technocratic politics was when big ideological conflict was over. But it’s just as historically specific to that time period as the whole universal liberal democracy argument.

paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Elliott Management has called on Australia’s largest gold producer to hold fresh talks with its potential suitor after the company rejected an A$39bn ($27bn) takeover offer from South Africa’s Gold Fields that would create the world’s second-largest miner of the precious metal.
The future of Northern Star Resources has been uncertain since US hedge fund Elliott called for the Perth-based gold producer toput itself up for salein June following a series of profit warnings.
Gold Fields, which was identified by Elliott as one of the only gold producers large enough to buy the company, has approached its rival on multiple occasions in recent months.

Northern Star said on Monday that it had rejected an offer from Gold Fields, one of the world’s largestgoldproducers and which already has significant operations in Australia, as “opportunistic, unsolicited and conditional”.

title: TotalEnergies boosts buybacks and dividends as oil prices surge
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

TotalEnergies raised its share buyback target for the fourth quarter and promised to increase dividends by more than 5 per cent annually until the end of the decade as the French major profits from soaring oil and gas prices.

Though Total’s oil and gas production was hit by theIran-US warthat began in February, the group is among those now receiving a boost from high prices and refining margins, while its output is also growing in other regions.
The company said on Monday that it now aimed for share buybacks of $2.5bn in the fourth quarter and between $2bn and $2.5bn in the first quarter of 2027.

That is up from $1.5bn in the July to September period, and marks a notable turnaround from late last year when, like its peers, Total was damping its outlook and warning of lower returns. Brent crude prices were then below $70 a barrel, compared with the current figure of above $100 a barrel.
Total chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said the outlook was a turnaround from the period before the Iran war “when everyone was very bearish”.
“We’ll increase the buyback in two steps” so as not do “$4bn in one quarter”, he told analysts. “There’s room for high returns to shareholders.”

Total said it would increase its dividend by more than 5 per cent a year between 2026 and 2030, while strongly increasing its free cash flow and reducing debt. The group also forecast a boom ahead for its electricity production, as it continues a pivot intorenewable energy, saying electric power would be 20 per cent of its energy mix by 2030.

“We say more oil and gas and more power,” Pouyanné said, acknowledging that the group was not looking to stop fossil-fuel investments for now even as it turned to electricity, which has drawn some criticism from activists.

Its update comes as higher prices at the pump risk sparking a political backlash, as opposition parties in France call for extra taxes on energy groups. The French government has rolled out targeted measures to help people relying on their cars for work, or on very modest wages, but has held off backing a windfall tax on the sector.
Total has been subsidising prices at its forecourts for several months in an effort to head off criticism and ease the situation for motorists, though this in turn has irked other distributors.

The company has a series of new liquefied natural gas projects coming online in the coming years and is adding new oil investments, including in Namibia, Libya, Mozambique and Papua New Guinea, though some of these have been beset by problems in the past, including security issues.
“On the growth front, investors will need to be confident on execution given a number of challenging projects in the hopper,” said Biraj Borkhataria, analyst at RBC Capital Markets.
Total shares closed up 0.8 per cent at €80.86.

title: Bond sell-off deepens and oil rises as Iran-US deal hopes fade
paragraphs: Kate Duguidin New York andEmily HerbertandIan Smithin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

US borrowing costs hit their highest level since the onset of the global financial crisis, as fading hopes of a deal between Washington and Tehran drove up oil prices and a sell-off in the Treasury market deepened.

Brent crude rose more than 4 per cent to a high of $108.83 a barrel on Monday, after US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, leaving no clear path to ending the seven-month war. Oil prices pared the gains later and settled 0.9 per cent higher at $105.28.

The renewed selling pressure onUS Treasuriessent yields on 10-year bonds up as much as 0.09 percentage points to 5.27 per cent, the highest since June 2007. Yields have risen for five consecutive sessions and are up more than 0.5 percentage points since mid-August, when Treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced an expanded bond buyback programme designed to calm the market.
The interest rate-sensitive US two-year yield also rose on Monday to 4.96 per cent, a 28-month high. Yields on both instruments backed off the highs in Monday afternoon trading.

“The potential fallout on the global economy from the war with Iran remains a key driver of the macro narrative,” said Ian Lyngen, head of US interest rate strategy at BMO Capital Markets. “There will, eventually, come a point at which the moves in energy will no longer have such an impact on US rates. Clearly, the market has yet to reach such an inflection point.”

Lyngen said that selling pressure on the 10-year Treasury could push its yield beyond 5.35 per cent before investors are incentivised to jump back into the market. Yields around that level would be at their highest in almost a quarter-century.
The rise in bond yields and oil prices also weighed on stocks, with the S&P 500 closing 0.8 per cent lower and the Nasdaq 100 dropping 1.1 per cent.

US borrowing costs have soared in recent weeks to levels not seen since before the global financial crisis, as signs of persistent inflation and strong growth in the world’s biggest economy have prompted investors to bet on higher interest rates.

The jump in yields has also pushed US mortgage rates above 7 per cent, as the bond sell-off translates into higher borrowing costs for Americans — just weeks before crucial midterm elections in which the country’s affordability crisis has become a central issue.
US voters have soured on Trump’s handling of the economy, sending his approval ratingssharply lower. Polls reveal deep voter disquiet about his war in Iran and its costs.

The Federal Reserve raised borrowing costs earlier this month for the first time since 2023, and investors in futures markets are betting on two more quarter-point rises by January — a marked shift from the cuts that had been expected before theUS-Iran warsent energy prices soaring.

Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chair of research at Barclays, said there was “nothing magical about these yield levels”, and it would take something substantial to reverse the sell-off, such as “if the US economy starts to slow down” or higher rates start “biting” risky assets such as stocks. “That would be one sign that we have perhaps gone far enough.”
UK government bonds also weakened further on Monday, with the 10-year gilt yield rising to 5.44 per cent — its highest level since 2007.
The sell-off on Monday also pushed French and Italian 10-year bond yields to fresh multiyear highs, with French borrowing costs at their highest level since 2008.
Other big central banks are also expected to make a series of rate rises in the coming months to contain a burst of inflation set off by the conflict.

Pooja Kumra, a rates strategist at TD Securities, said the bond sell-off was being powered by a combination of “persistent economic resilience” and the lack of a roadmap to “how the war might be resolved”, which was pushing investors to bet on rates remaining higher for longer.

Paul Watters, head of European credit research at S&P Global Ratings, said: “Our sense is that [bond] yields could grind higher” from here, in part because “we see the energy price shock continuing through 2027”.
“The buffers are eroding” in global energy reserves, Watters pointed out, referring to countries using up their stockpiles.

title: Burford Capital could gain up to $1.4bn from Apple patent defeat
paragraphs: Stefania Palmain London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Litigation funder Burford Capital said it stands to gain up to $1.4bn after a US federal jury ruled against Apple in a major technology patent case.
Burford on Monday said it had a “financial entitlement” in what it described as “one of the largest patent verdicts in US history”, sending shares up 9 per cent in early trading in London.

A jury in a San Diego court on Friday awarded $5.7bn in damages to Taction Technology, which develops vibration technology for electronic devices, and which sued Apple in 2021 for allegedly using its “patented inventions without license or authority”.

Taction accusedAppleof violating two of its patents concerning the haptic feedback in iPhones and Apple Watches in its legal complaint, alleging that the tech giant had capitalised on its “innovation and success” by selling the devices.

The company argued that Apple’s “Taptic Engine,” which is embedded in many of its products, unlawfully used its inventions. Apple denied the claim as “invalid” in its own legal filings, arguing that Taction had introduced insufficient evidence and rejecting accusations of wilful or indirect infringement.

Apple has pledged to appeal against the verdict and said in a statement: “While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today’s verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts.”

It added that its Taptic Engine was “fundamentally different from Taction’s technology, which Taction’s own testing of Apple’s products confirmed during trial.” Taction did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Taction’s win on Friday follows abig lossfor Burford in March, when a US appeals court overturned a ruling that found Argentina liable to pay $16bn to former shareholders of the oil major YPF.

The litigation funder had backed the shareholders’ claims and would have taken a share of the award. Its shares fell as much as 54 per cent in New York in the wake of the ruling — at the time its biggest intraday decline since July 2020.

Burfordon Monday cautioned that the Apple verdict did not “represent a final judgment or cash proceeds received by” the litigation funder. It said post-trial proceedings, including efforts by Apple to overturn the jury’s verdict, could leave Burford recovering “substantially less” than $1.4bn or, “in certain circumstances, [incurring] a total loss”.
“As with all litigation, the outcome remains uncertain until final resolution, and there can be no assurance as to the timing or amount of any ultimate recovery,” Burford added.
