title: What is the AI capex breakeven rate?
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026

You might have heard that the AI hyperscalers are spending squillions on building data centres. The scale is now transforming debt markets, and not unreasonably this is raising some concerns about the boom’s durability.
As PGIM Fixed Income’s Greg Peters said in today’s (very good)FT Big Read:
The overarching narrative is — anywhere and everywhere. The quantum of debt that is hitting the marketplace is historic. The numbers are just absolutely enormous. It’s transformational.
Whether this is sustainable comes down to how much money these data centres are able to generate, and — ultimately — how much money AI as a whole will be able to generate.

Last month, Dan Davies crunched the numbers onAnthropic’s lease of SpaceX’s excess data centre capacityand concluded that data centre leasing is currently a wildly profitable business, even with extremely conservative assumptions on depreciation and construction costs.

But the calculus might look radically different when more compute comes online in the coming years, or, say, ifless compute-intensive open-models gain ground. So how much money do we all need to spend on AI tools for the hyperscaler capex splurge to actually make money?

Luckily, several economists have been crunching the numbers lately to figure out exactly this, albeit with subtly different perspectives and assumptions. Let’s start with Goldman Sachs’ estimates. In a report last week it said:

Outlook for AI capex:The largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capex in 2026 and consensus expects $1.1 trillion in spending in 2027. Our baseline forecast is that capex spending will increase in 2027 and surpass consensus estimates but the rate of both capex growth and upside surprises will diminish relative to recent quarters.

What capex signals about required AI revenues:Based on average annual capex in 2026 and 2027, our equity analysts estimate that the hyperscalers need to generate annual AI revenues of roughly $300 billion in the next few years to break even on their investments. Hyperscaler cloud revenues have accelerated sharply this year, annualizing roughly $70 billion above the pre-AI trend in Q2 2026, and announced revenue backlogs exceed $1.5 trillion.

OK, so cloud computing AI revenues need to quickly increase by about 4x for the hyperscalers to simply break even on their investments. That seems punchy, but as Goldman points out, these revenues are now accelerating sharply.

However, to generate a return on investment capital of 30 per cent — at the lowest end of what the hyperscalers generated in the pre-hyperscale era — these data centres soon need to generate annual revenues of about $636bn. That’s more like 10x the current run rate.
Sure, the combined cloud revenue backlog of Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft is now $1.7tn, but Alphaville is a little less convinced by the firmness of this number than Goldman’s analysts.

Moreover, this is just what the underlying cloud-computing layer needs to generate. Then there are all the applications that sit on top of it, which presumably also want to actually make money at some point.

Goldman estimates that if these companies expect earnings margins of about 30 per cent — and the hyperscalers only generate a 10-20 per cent return on their capex — then the overall AI software spend is a bit over $1tn. Compared to a roughly $1.5tn global software spend, this seems ambitious but not fantastical.

However, if the hyperscalers are keen on a ROIC at least within touching distance of their historical norms, and AI software companies want margins closer to what software has historically generated, then consumer and enterprise spending needs to jump to nearly $2tn.

That seems . . . less feasible. Once consumers are used to a free or near-free product, hitting them with the full-fat cost of producing it is very difficult, as anyone experienced in the digital media industry can ruefully tell you.
On the same topic, here is afascinating recent paperby Columbia Business School’s Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Given the $8.2bn cost to build a 200-megawatt AI data centre — and the 183 gigawatts supposed to come online by 2032 — he estimates that the cumulative cost will clock in at over $10tn between 2025 and 2032 (which includes some spending on projects that will be finished after that point).

This is the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of GDP each year, a bigger capex splurge than those on canals, railroads, electricity and the internet in previous eras. “It would double the electricity consumption of the entire US residential sector,” Van Nieuwerburgh notes.

Assuming a modest 10 per cent unlevered return, a 50 per cent cash flow margin and a generous six-year life for the chips, he estimates that this will require annualised revenues of $3.7tn by 2032, or about 9.2 per cent of estimated US GDP at that point.
This is similar to the estimates of Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings, published in the former’sSubstacklast week:

Revenues would need to be between $2.4 trillion (if they simply broke even on the investments) and $3.8 trillion (if they needed to match the return they receive on their existing businesses) over the next six years. This is equivalent to their current incremental AI revenues increasing between 13-45 times in just six years (the range depends on revenue flow assumptions).

To make up for their relatively slow start, the hyperscalers need to quickly become hyper-profitable. Just in the next year, they’d need to post revenues between $520-850 billion, roughly three to four-and-a-half times what we estimate they made this year. If we strip out circular revenues—those from a firm in which the lab has an ownership stake—the future revenues must be even higher.

There are a lot of assumptions you could fiddle with to change the calculus, such as how firm the capex plans are, whether construction costs go up and down, token costs, the margin expectations of various layers in the AI ecosystem, demand from consumers and enterprise etc etc. Revenues are clearly growing at a remarkable rate right now, encouraging the optimists.
But the overall conclusion seems pretty clear: AI revenues very soon need to grow a LOT MORE for the size of these investment plans to make economic sense.

You might have heard that the AI hyperscalers are spending squillions on building data centres. The scale is now transforming debt markets, and not unreasonably this is raising some concerns about the boom’s durability.

As PGIM Fixed Income’s Greg Peters said in today’s (very good)FT Big Read:

The overarching narrative is — anywhere and everywhere. The quantum of debt that is hitting the marketplace is historic. The numbers are just absolutely enormous. It’s transformational.

Whether this is sustainable comes down to how much money these data centres are able to generate, and — ultimately — how much money AI as a whole will be able to generate.

Last month, Dan Davies crunched the numbers onAnthropic’s lease of SpaceX’s excess data centre capacityand concluded that data centre leasing is currently a wildly profitable business, even with extremely conservative assumptions on depreciation and construction costs.

But the calculus might look radically different when more compute comes online in the coming years, or, say, ifless compute-intensive open-models gain ground. So how much money do we all need to spend on AI tools for the hyperscaler capex splurge to actually make money?

Luckily, several economists have been crunching the numbers lately to figure out exactly this, albeit with subtly different perspectives and assumptions. Let’s start with Goldman Sachs’ estimates. In a report last week it said:

Outlook for AI capex:The largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capex in 2026 and consensus expects $1.1 trillion in spending in 2027. Our baseline forecast is that capex spending will increase in 2027 and surpass consensus estimates but the rate of both capex growth and upside surprises will diminish relative to recent quarters.

What capex signals about required AI revenues:Based on average annual capex in 2026 and 2027, our equity analysts estimate that the hyperscalers need to generate annual AI revenues of roughly $300 billion in the next few years to break even on their investments. Hyperscaler cloud revenues have accelerated sharply this year, annualizing roughly $70 billion above the pre-AI trend in Q2 2026, and announced revenue backlogs exceed $1.5 trillion.

OK, so cloud computing AI revenues need to quickly increase by about 4x for the hyperscalers to simply break even on their investments. That seems punchy, but as Goldman points out, these revenues are now accelerating sharply.

However, to generate a return on investment capital of 30 per cent — at the lowest end of what the hyperscalers generated in the pre-hyperscale era — these data centres soon need to generate annual revenues of about $636bn. That’s more like 10x the current run rate.

Sure, the combined cloud revenue backlog of Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft is now $1.7tn, but Alphaville is a little less convinced by the firmness of this number than Goldman’s analysts.

Moreover, this is just what the underlying cloud-computing layer needs to generate. Then there are all the applications that sit on top of it, which presumably also want to actually make money at some point.

Goldman estimates that if these companies expect earnings margins of about 30 per cent — and the hyperscalers only generate a 10-20 per cent return on their capex — then the overall AI software spend is a bit over $1tn. Compared to a roughly $1.5tn global software spend, this seems ambitious but not fantastical.

However, if the hyperscalers are keen on a ROIC at least within touching distance of their historical norms, and AI software companies want margins closer to what software has historically generated, then consumer and enterprise spending needs to jump to nearly $2tn.

That seems . . . less feasible. Once consumers are used to a free or near-free product, hitting them with the full-fat cost of producing it is very difficult, as anyone experienced in the digital media industry can ruefully tell you.

On the same topic, here is afascinating recent paperby Columbia Business School’s Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Given the $8.2bn cost to build a 200-megawatt AI data centre — and the 183 gigawatts supposed to come online by 2032 — he estimates that the cumulative cost will clock in at over $10tn between 2025 and 2032 (which includes some spending on projects that will be finished after that point).

This is the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of GDP each year, a bigger capex splurge than those on canals, railroads, electricity and the internet in previous eras. “It would double the electricity consumption of the entire US residential sector,” Van Nieuwerburgh notes.

Assuming a modest 10 per cent unlevered return, a 50 per cent cash flow margin and a generous six-year life for the chips, he estimates that this will require annualised revenues of $3.7tn by 2032, or about 9.2 per cent of estimated US GDP at that point.

This is similar to the estimates of Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings, published in the former’sSubstacklast week:

Revenues would need to be between $2.4 trillion (if they simply broke even on the investments) and $3.8 trillion (if they needed to match the return they receive on their existing businesses) over the next six years. This is equivalent to their current incremental AI revenues increasing between 13-45 times in just six years (the range depends on revenue flow assumptions).

To make up for their relatively slow start, the hyperscalers need to quickly become hyper-profitable. Just in the next year, they’d need to post revenues between $520-850 billion, roughly three to four-and-a-half times what we estimate they made this year. If we strip out circular revenues—those from a firm in which the lab has an ownership stake—the future revenues must be even higher.

There are a lot of assumptions you could fiddle with to change the calculus, such as how firm the capex plans are, whether construction costs go up and down, token costs, the margin expectations of various layers in the AI ecosystem, demand from consumers and enterprise etc etc. Revenues are clearly growing at a remarkable rate right now, encouraging the optimists.

But the overall conclusion seems pretty clear: AI revenues very soon need to grow a LOT MORE for the size of these investment plans to make economic sense.

title: Nvidia launches record $150bn share buyback
paragraphs: Tim Bradshawin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
Nvidia is launching the biggest share buyback in US corporate history as the Silicon Valley chipmaker continues to reap huge profits from its perch at the top of the AI supply chain.
The world’s most valuable company said on Monday that its board had approved a $150bn increase to its buyback programme, eclipsing the record $110bn set by Apple in 2024.
Nvidiais now authorised to spend up to $235bn on share buybacks before January 2028.

Nvidia’s profits are surging as the tech industry continues to pour enormous sums into AI infrastructure, with Goldman Sachs forecasting that AI investment will exceed $1tn this year. Its chips are the workhorses of the large language models that power ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

The company’s shares have risen more than 1,200 per cent since OpenAI debuted ChatGPT in late 2022. But the stock’s extraordinary momentum has slowed in 2026, rising about 20 per cent in the year to date, as more investors question the sustainability of the AI boom.
Shares in Nvidia jumped 3 per cent in early trading on Monday.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and chief executive, said on Monday that its new plan reflected “confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead” from AI.

“Nvidia’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing,” Huang said. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders.”

Large buyback authorisations often indicate that a company’s management believes its shares are undervalued. But large capital returns are typically associated with a slowdown in growth for large, well-established companies.

When Apple announced its $110bn buyback in 2024, the iPhone maker held all of the top five spots for the largest such authorisations by a US company, according to Bloomberg. At the time, the iPhone’s growth was slowing but Apple continued to reap huge profits from its dominance of the smartphone market.

By contrast, Nvidia’s salescontinue to riserapidly. Its revenues are forecast to grow about 90 per cent this year. Fierce competitors in the AI race, including OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX, are all huge customers. Even Google, which has its own range of AI chips, is a big buyer of Nvidia’s products through its cloud computing unit.

Nvidia generated almost $100bn in free cash flow in its most recent financial year ending in January. That figure is forecast to more than triple to $329bn in fiscal 2028, according to consensus estimates from S&P Global’s Visible Alpha.
The chipmaker’s net income is forecast to more than double to $245bn in the current financial year, according to Visible Alpha, rising to $387bn in the following fiscal year ending in January 2028.

title: Meta launches enterprise AI business seeking to cash in on vast spending
paragraphs: Rafe Rosner-Uddinin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026

Meta is launching a new business selling AI tools to enterprise customers, as chief executive Mark Zuckerberg seeks new ways to generate returns from the company’s enormous investment in the technology.

The parent of Facebook and Instagram on Monday said that the new arm would bring together products including itsMuse personal assistantand coding tools, alongside access to its advanced AI models.Chirantan “CJ” Desai, chief executive of database group MongoDB, will helm the new business unit and report directly to Zuckerberg.

“We are starting the next major pillar of our business, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help businesses use AI to grow and transform in new ways as well,” said Zuckerberg in a statement.The move comes as Zuckerberg seeks to turn Meta’s vast spending on artificial intelligence into new sources of revenue beyond its core advertising business. The company plans to spend as much as $145bn in capital expenditure this year, much of it on the data centre infrastructure and advanced models underpinning its AI push.

Meta’sshares have rallied sharply in recent weeks as the success of Muse, its new AI assistant, has helped shift investor sentiment towards Zuckerberg’s spending spree. The app, the development of which was first revealed by the FT in May, has quickly become the most downloaded app on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US since its launch at the beginning of September.That rally reversed on Monday, with Meta shares falling 4 per cent following the announcement of its new enterprise arm. MongoDB shares dropped nearly 20 per cent after Desai’s departure was announced.Zuckerberg has insisted that Meta’s AI investments will bolster its core advertising business while creating new profit engines.
The easy-to-use Muse app offers consumers a team of autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries, booking travel and organising finances.

Zuckerberg last week unveiled a new handheld AI “charm” device that will feature Muse, alongside a range of new capabilities including the ability to have live conversations with the interactive AI assistant.The Meta chief has previously discussed selling excess data centre capacity to customers, in a move that would see the company compete with cloud computing giants including Amazon and Microsoft.

On Monday, Zuckerberg told investors that the group would “use our strengths” including vast data centre infrastructure in a push to serve enterprise customers. He did not state whether the company had immediate plans to sell excess capacity to customers, similar to rival SpaceX, which has signed deals with Anthropic and Google.

“Meta Enterprise Platform will focus on turning its AI stack into products and services that companies can deploy for their own businesses,” Desai said. “Our goal is to make Meta the place enterprises come to scale their businesses.”

title: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s AI start-up for $8bn
paragraphs: Michael Actonin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026

AMD has agreed to acquire AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s start-up World Labs for $8.2bn in an all-stock transaction that will push the Nvidia competitor further beyond chips into cutting-edge model development.

Li, the Stanford University researcher described as the “godmother of artificial intelligence”, founded the company in 2024 to work on so-called world models, AI systems that can understand and replicate 3D environments.
AMD’s chief executive Lisa Su said the deal would help the near-$1tn chip designer “shape its future technology road maps” by giving it insight into how the uses forAIare evolving.
BothAMDand its chief rival Nvidia are expanding beyond semiconductors into AI model development, using their huge earnings from hardware sales in recent years.

Nvidia, which builds its own models, earlier this month announced a $13bn deal to buy AI platform Hugging Face. It has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to start-up investments, debt guarantees and financial backstops across the AI sector.

AMD’s deal for San Francisco-based World Labs, which it expects to close by the end of 2026 pending regulatory approval, gives it a foothold in world models, which have potential applications in industries such as robotics and gaming.

World models, trained on images, video and text, are widely considered one of the next frontiers in AI beyond the large language models behind tools such as ChatGPT. Former Meta AI chief Yann LeCun left the company late last year to launchhis own start-upfocused on world models.

“Advancing the next generation of AI technology requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute,” said Li. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI.”
Li, who is best known for founding ImageNet, a database that became the foundation of modern computer vision technology, will join AMD as executive vice-president and chief scientist.

Li said in a blog post that “without a focused hardware, AI is hobbled in efficiency”. The two companies partnered last year to train models on AMD’s chips and discovered they were a “natural fit”, she wrote.
AMD invested in World Labs as part of a $1bn fundraising in February that included Nvidia, at a reported $5bn valuation. Andreessen Horowitz is among the start-up’s early backers.

AMD has made acquisitions over recent years as it looks to build its hardware and software ecosystem. These include its $4.4bn acquisition of ZT Systems in 2025 and the $665mn acquisition of Finnish AI model company Silo AI in 2024.

It has also agreed deals to supply chips to leading AI model makers, offering up its equity to secure long-term purchase commitments. In February, AMD struck a multibillion-dollar chip supply deal with Meta, with a provision for the social media group to take up to a 10 per cent stake in the company over time. An October 2025 deal with OpenAI included a similar share arrangement.
AMD announced it would invest up to $5bn in OpenAI’s main rival Anthropic as it commits to buying tens of billions of dollars of AMD’s AI data centre chips.
The World Labs deal comes as AMD and its rivals expect a new phase of massive growth from AI in robotics, with the companies developing specialised chips for these purposes.
The companies are also experimenting with new chip architectures that could start to displace the graphics processing units that dominated the first phase of AI computing.

Nvidia paid $20bn in December 2025 to hire top executives and licence technology from start-up Groq, which developed a specialised accelerator chip aimed at running AI models faster than current hardware. Nvidia incorporated this technology into a new product this year. In August, AMD announced it was acquiring specialised chip company Taalas.

title: Pope Leo criticises Nvidia’s Jensen Huang over AI safety
paragraphs: Michael Actonin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Pope Leo XIV has rebuked Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang for downplaying the risks posed by AI, saying concerns about the threat the technology poses to humanity should be taken seriously.

Huang, along with US President Donald Trump, has rejected calls from frontierAIlabs OpenAI and Anthropic to co-ordinate and slow model development and introduce more regulation following a series of high-profile hacking incidents and public warnings about the technology’s existential risks.
Pope Leo told reporters he had read reports about Nvidia launching new safety tools for model builders on Monday but questioned Huang’s commitment to safety in light of his recent comments.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” PopeLeosaid on the flight back to Rome from a visit to France.
“I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously,” he added.
Pope Leo criticises Nvidia chief over AI safety

The Pope’s swipe at the leader of the world’s most valuable company testifies to the extraordinary level of concern around AI safety issues, which have become a top priority for leaders around the world.
OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei appeared at the UN Security Council last week to address the issue and argue for greater global co-operation.

But the push for international action on AI guardrails has been stalled by Trump, who has called warnings that the technology could threaten humanity a “hoax” and rejected any “globalist scheme of control of superintelligence”.
Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump on several occasions, said AI anxiety was not “fake news, as some have said”.
“If someone were to ask me: ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No, I’m not. I sleep at night,” Pope Leo said. “This is a problem that I think we need to sit down and talk about.”

The pontiff’s comment about Nvidia comes after the $5.5tn chipmaker unveiled a new set of security tools aimed at policing the activity of AI agents — bots that can operate autonomously — including a system called “Sentry” that tracks agent behaviour using Nvidia’s “data processing unit” chips.
An Nvidia executive told reporters the tools would have prevented a high-profile hack of Hugging Face in July by OpenAI agents that triggered fresh debate about the risks AI poses.
“It’s interesting to note that, just today, I read that the head of Nvidia claims that he has found some way of inserting into AI certain guardrails,” Pope Leo said.

Since assuming the papacy last year, Chicago-born Pope Leo has shown a close interest in AI. In May heissued a formal letterknown as an “encyclical” in which he said AI was not morally neutral and must be “disarmed” through robust regulation to ensure it serves humanity rather than undermine it.
Last week it emerged that OpenAI’s models had hacked dozens of websites, including an Australian health service website, during the course of routine training runs.

The Nvidia chief has spent recent weeks joining forces with Trump to argue against the need for additional regulation or oversight, emphasising that the responsibility to ensure safety lies with the individual companies.
“The market forces are already there. We don’t need any new laws. We don’t need new regulations,” Huang said earlier this month.
Huang, who has become one of the closest tech executives to Trump, took a call from the president onstage at an event in which he agreed that the concerns amounted to a hoax.
Pope Leo’s intervention comes as leading AI executives are set to meet Trump and US lawmakers at the White House on Tuesday.
Trump dined with Amodei on Sunday night, in a sign of détente with the company after the Pentagon banned its products when Anthropic tried to restrict their use in warfare.
Nvidia declined to comment.

title: Singapore’s bet on chipmaking
paragraphs: Owen Walkerin Singapore
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
Singapore’s ambitions to seize more of the global chip industry are limited only by its size, according to Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Last month Wong announced a project for the city-state to merge several of its smaller islands into a bigger piece of reclaimed land, saying it could “help shape Singapore for the next 50 years” by supporting a new generation of industries, including advanced manufacturing.
While best known as a trading and finance hub,Singaporehas also become a key producer of the semiconductors that drive the global economy.

On Monday VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — a joint venture between Taiwan’s Vanguard and Dutch chipmaker NXP — opened its doors on a $7.8bn plant, becoming the latest high-tech company in the country.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, VSMC chair Leuh Fang said the company was even considering opening a second plant in Singapore in order to meet the high levels of demand.

Singapore’s economy has this year been turbocharged by chips and other advanced manufacturing, from medical devices to aerospace components and speciality chemicals. The global AI boom, in particular, has been a boon for its chipmakers.

“Singapore has done very well in becoming an established base for this emerging area of growth,” said Tan Yew Kong, general manager of Asia-Pacific manufacturing at GlobalFoundries, one of the chipmakers in Singapore. “AI is booming and Singapore has an advantage.”

The country makes one in 10 of the world’ssemiconductors— though a smaller share of the most advanced chips — and a fifth of the machinery that makes them, according to the country’s Economic Development Board. The industry accounts for nearly 7 per cent of Singapore’s GDP.

Singapore had its strongest first-half trade performance since 2010, according to Moody’s, and growth has been higher in the two months since. Electronics exports surged 132 per cent in August compared with a year earlier, while shipments of personal computers — including server racks used in data centres — rose 238 per cent.

Between 2022 and 2025, Singapore attracted more than $23.5bn in semiconductor investments. Among the companies that have set up fabrication plants to make chips are Micron, Infineon, Siltronic and UMC. Applied Materials opened a$500mn campusin June.

title: Will Adani get an airline?
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 29 2026
This article is an on-site version of the India Business Briefing newsletter. To receive it in your inbox regularly,sign upif you’re a premium subscriber or upgrade your subscriptionhere.

Good morning. This promises to be an eventful week, with the Cockroach Janta Party calling on the country’syouth to protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over mass deletions from the electoral rolls. They are timing the march for Mahatma Gandhi’s birth anniversary (since Friday is a public holiday, there will be no India Business Briefing).
In today’s newsletter, the insurance regulator has proposed mega changes to fees and commissions for policy sales. But first, the intrigue and drama around the possible prospect of an Adani Airlines.
TheAdani Groupand the government appear to be engaged in an intricate tango over the group’s airline ambitions.

The issue first surfaced in July, when media reports suggested Adani was seeking a waiver from a rule that prevents the group, as the operator of Mumbai’s main airport, from holding more than 10 per cent of shares in a scheduled airline. At the time, Adani Enterprises, the group flagship company, strongly denied that it had plans to enter the airline business, telling the stock exchanges that reports otherwise were “entirely baseless”. The following day, however, The Economic Times reported that Arun Bansal, chief executive of Adani Airport Holdings, had asked the Airports Authority of India to waive the restriction in a letter on June 4. The letter said group company Adani Defence & Aerospace was evaluating the possibility of starting an airline as a natural extension of its aviation business.

Cut to last week. Speaking at an industry event in Delhi, civil aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu said the government was examining the pros and cons of allowing airport operators to run airlines. He said it would be cautious given the conflict of interest that cross-ownership creates, but also made clear it wants more competition in a market where IndiGo and Air India account for more than 90 per cent of domestic traffic. The Times of India last week quoted Bansal saying that “as airport CEO” he would “not like to” compete with his own customers. I asked Adani Enterprises at the weekend about the group’s intentions, but did not hear back in time for this newsletter.

It is worth noting that the restriction itself dates back to the 2006 privatisation of the Mumbai and Delhi airports. It was written into the specific agreements between the government and operators, and is not a blanket rule that is applied to every airport in the country.

IndiGo co-founder and managing director Rahul Bhatia has vehemently opposed any relaxation. Bhatia sees airport operators owning airlines as a “massive conflict of interest”, sincethey control access to critical infrastructuresuch as airport slots and parking bays. He has also pointed out that there is no global precedent for an arrangement he says could ultimately hurt consumers.

Several things are at play here. The government has to tread carefully because the company at the centre of the debate isAdani, one of India’s most high-profile business groups. Any relaxation of a rule that could directly benefit it is therefore likely to attract political scrutiny.
At the same time, the government has a legitimate argument for wanting more competition. BothAir IndiaandIndiGo have had their own troublesin the past year.

The question, then, is whether the government can devise a framework that addresses the conflict-of-interest concerns while allowing new capital into an industry dominated by two groups. It will be interesting to see whether a cabinet decision emerges.

India’s insurance regulator is proposing sweeping changes in the commissions and fees paid to sell policies. In a consultation paper published last week, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) proposed capping payouts to intermediaries and distributors, and reversing its own 2023 decision to free up the commission structure. The caps vary by product type and by the term over which premiums are paid. It is a complicated structure, depending on the nature of the product and the duration of the policy, but roughly the proposed mandate would cut maximum commissions to 15 per cent for life insurers from as high as 26.7 per cent for some, and to 20 per cent for non-life policies from up to 30 per cent.

There are several reasons for the regulator to change its mind on commissions and fees. The sector isopening to foreign capital, and Irdai wants commissions to better reflect business realities. Products with single-premium payments, or those that have tax benefits, basically sell themselves without big incentives. Irdai’s analysis of 2023-25 data found distributor payouts grew 125 per cent, but premiums grew only 28 per cent. This makes it an inefficient incentive structure.

The changes, if implemented, would hit financial services firms whose revenue leans heavily on insurance sales, and large Indian banks, for whom insurance commissions are a sizeable share of retail income — as high as 10 per cent of fee income for some. PB Fintech, the parent of Policybazaar, a listed insurance seller, told analysts its non-life insurance business could lose up to two-thirds of its value if the proposals went through. The company’s stock fell more than 36 per cent on the publication of the consultation paper, erasing over Rs314bn in market capitalisation.

Mouthwatering incentives have fuelled rampant mis-selling, with agents steering clients towards whichever policy pays the highest commission rather than the one that best suits their needs. Irdai’s changes also aim to reward persistence and encourage distributors to keep clients paying premiums rather than lapsing mid-policy. These reforms are expected to make insurance cheaper, though that depends on how much of the savings insurers actually pass on. The Indian insurance industry has grown increasingly customer-unfriendly in recent years, with complaints piling up over denied claims. This is especially true in health insurance, where some insurers’ claim settlement ratio is as low as 82 per cent. The proposed changes should improve the competitive landscape, as sellers will not be incentivised by disproportionate commissions. Feedback on the consultation paper is open until October 25.

This is largely because the country is unable to create enough jobs for its graduates.

title: Convenience store woman: Lady Gaga urges Japanese to work at FamilyMart
paragraphs: Harry DempseyandLeo Lewisin Tokyo
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
Japanese convenience store chain FamilyMart has enlisted global pop megastar Lady Gaga as it ratchets up its staff recruitment efforts to offset the country’s acute labour shortage.

In a commercial that aired this week, the American singer, clad in a custom navy leather uniform and white platform stilettos, hands outfamichikifried chicken and mops the floors of a monochrome convenience store.

The 30-second spot is the convenience store chain’s latest effort to entice more part-time staff to join its ranks, as Japan’s corporate giants pour increasing resources into advertising budgets and recruitment efforts to battle a nationwide labour shortage.

“Why not work at FamilyMart,” Lady Gaga asks viewers in Japanese as she struts down an aisle past two android-looking versions of herself, restocking shelves with products including cup noodles, snacks and curry packets.
Lady Gaga's FamilyMart advert

“This must be the first time that a convenience store has used a famous celebrity to promote the idea of working there. Usually, the ads are for new products or discount campaigns,” said Masuji Ikeda, senior researcher at the Distribution Economics Institute of Japan. “It’s a turning point.”
Lady Gagais immensely popular in Japan, respectfully dubbed “Gaga-sama” by fans and selling out all six January dates of her Mayhem Ball tour in the country.

Convenience stores and their franchisees, which rely on part-time labour, arestruggling to attract staff, for whom 24/7 operations, low wages and gruelling work offer little appeal, and at a time when a shrinking workforce is beginning to give workers more leverage and inflation is eating into profit margins.
Advertising professionals said the Lady Gaga tie-in reflected a broader shift within corporate Japan.

“More and more [clients] are telling us that the only point of marketing for us is now recruitment,” said an executive at Hakuhodo, one of Japan’s major advertising agencies. “What they need above everything is for people to know their company name so that they will think about working for them.”
They added: “This is advertising for people, because that is what they need most.”

A spokesperson forFamilyMart, which is currently advertising 10,481 part-time jobs across 16,455 stores in Japan, told the FT that the Lady Gaga campaign was the latest in a series of efforts to make its workplace more appealing, fun and exciting to potential jobseekers.
The convenience store chain has refreshed its uniform for the first time in a decade, debuting a more modern, casual style and colour scheme at a catwalk show at Tokyo’s premier sumo venue in August.

Convenience chains have also led the charge onaccepting more foreign workersto fill staffing gaps — one solution to Japan’s demographic crisis that traditional industries have resisted. They have also introduced more technology, necessitating a more tech-savvy workforce.

Family Mart in particular has come under pressure froma sales slowdownover the past year as customer traffic has fallen, which could hamper franchises’ ability to pay higher wages and attract and retain staff.
FamilyMart is the second biggest among Japan’s three leading convenience store chains, with ¥3.3tn ($21bn) of annual revenue.

This year, 7-Eleven, the sector’s largest player, announced the first comprehensive overhaul in half a century of its franchise agreements, lowering the royalties paid to head office and giving franchisees more wriggle room to increase part-time wages.
FamilyMart said it was not working on any such plans. The company declined to comment on the cost of the Lady Gaga campaign.

title: US Treasury threatens crackdown on Wall Street tax-avoidance strategies
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
The US Treasury on Monday took its first concrete steps towards cracking down on a suite of strategies used by wealthy US investors to cut their tax bills.
The department warned that it could clamp down on “potentially abusive” tactics and issued a ruling targeting the aggressive use of ETFs to avoid taxable gains.
It said in a notice it was probing the use of strategies that “purport to produce tax results that may be inconsistent with the purpose and proper application of the relevant federal tax rules”.

In an accompanying ruling, the Internal Revenue Service targeted a strategy known as the 351 conversion, which allows investors with appreciated assets to rebalance their portfolios without incurring taxable gains.
“This is a seismic moment in the ETF market,” said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst and editor of the Tax Alpha Insider newsletter.

Strategies that help wealthy Americans minimise theirtaxbills have surged in popularity in recent years, aided by a US stock market boom that has shifted the focus for some investors towards “tax alpha”, or gains derived from lowering tax liabilities.

Hedge funds offering tax alpha strategies accruedmore than $90bnbetween the start of 2025 and April this year, according to FT calculations. Since 2021, ETFs created using 351 conversions have raised a total of at least $21bn, according to Tax Alpha Insider.

The 351 conversion is one of several strategies that take advantage of the favourable tax treatment ofETFs, which US investors can usually use to avoid paying capital gains tax by trading “in kind” with market makers so that no cash changes hands.
But in a ruling on Monday the IRS said it would treat some of these transactions as taxable exchanges.

“Our message on these conversions is clear: they don’t work under existing law,” Treasury secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” he added.

Sullivan said the ruling targeted cases in which “someone contributes a portfolio of securities that is out of step with the ETF’s prospectus and then quickly washes those securities via in-kind redemption”.
He cautioned: “It’s going to come down to the facts and circumstances of each case” and added that the ruling would not “kill . . . routine tax planning” that involves the 351 conversion.
The Treasury’s notice said it was seeking further information on a series of “strategies used by tax-aware funds” together with a list of ETF manoeuvres including the 351 conversion.

The written notice marks the Treasury’s first escalation since it signalled its interest in probing tax strategies at an industry event in July, where officials warned they would not turn “a blind eye to aggressive planning”.

The Treasury added it was “also considering issuing additional guidance or taking other action to address the transactions described in this notice” and that such guidance could apply “retroactively”.
Shares in Affiliated Managers Group, which owns a stake in AQR, a pioneer of the latest breed of tax-aware investing strategies, fell as much as 2 per cent on Monday.

AQR is, by some estimates, the largest hedge fund in the world. Together with rival Quantinno, it popularised an approach that uses leverage and algorithmic trading to buy and short securities at scale, and to systematically realise losses on positions.
AQR said previously that the “primary draw for investors” should be the returns from its strategies — the “pre-tax alpha”, or market-beating performance — before any tax benefits.

In an accompanying ruling, the Internal Revenue Service targeted a strategy known as the 351 conversion, which allows investors with appreciated assets to rebalance their portfolios without incurring taxable gains.

“This is a seismic moment in the ETF market,” said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst and editor of the Tax Alpha Insider newsletter.

Strategies that help wealthy Americans minimise theirtaxbills have surged in popularity in recent years, aided by a US stock market boom that has shifted the focus for some investors towards “tax alpha”, or gains derived from lowering tax liabilities.

Hedge funds offering tax alpha strategies accruedmore than $90bnbetween the start of 2025 and April this year, according to FT calculations. Since 2021, ETFs created using 351 conversions have raised a total of at least $21bn, according to Tax Alpha Insider.

The 351 conversion is one of several strategies that take advantage of the favourable tax treatment ofETFs, which US investors can usually use to avoid paying capital gains tax by trading “in kind” with market makers so that no cash changes hands.

But in a ruling on Monday the IRS said it would treat some of these transactions as taxable exchanges.

“Our message on these conversions is clear: they don’t work under existing law,” Treasury secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” he added.

Sullivan said the ruling targeted cases in which “someone contributes a portfolio of securities that is out of step with the ETF’s prospectus and then quickly washes those securities via in-kind redemption”.

He cautioned: “It’s going to come down to the facts and circumstances of each case” and added that the ruling would not “kill . . . routine tax planning” that involves the 351 conversion.

The Treasury’s notice said it was seeking further information on a series of “strategies used by tax-aware funds” together with a list of ETF manoeuvres including the 351 conversion.

The written notice marks the Treasury’s first escalation since it signalled its interest in probing tax strategies at an industry event in July, where officials warned they would not turn “a blind eye to aggressive planning”.

The Treasury added it was “also considering issuing additional guidance or taking other action to address the transactions described in this notice” and that such guidance could apply “retroactively”.

Shares in Affiliated Managers Group, which owns a stake in AQR, a pioneer of the latest breed of tax-aware investing strategies, fell as much as 2 per cent on Monday.

AQR is, by some estimates, the largest hedge fund in the world. Together with rival Quantinno, it popularised an approach that uses leverage and algorithmic trading to buy and short securities at scale, and to systematically realise losses on positions.

AQR said previously that the “primary draw for investors” should be the returns from its strategies — the “pre-tax alpha”, or market-beating performance — before any tax benefits.

title: OpenAI axes next model citing safety issues
paragraphs: Ryan McMorrowandGeorge Hammondin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 29 2026

OpenAI has pulled the release of its next AI model, saying it performed worse than its predecessor on safety evaluations as the industry grapples with a spate of incidents in which AI agents hacked into other companies and governments.
Saachi Jain, head of safety systems atOpenAI, said the company decided to hold back GPT-6.1 Astra after the model “didn’t quite meet the bar” for staying within the bounds of its instructions.

The announcement comes after OpenAI last week said it had notified dozens of partners, including governments, that its AI agents had breached their systems and that agents had inadvertently leaked more than 50 images shared by users to image-hosting sites.
This marked the latest in a series of disclosures about misbehaviour and hacking by OpenAI’s AI agents — bots that can perform complex tasks autonomously.
The $852bn start-up has acknowledged that in some cases it took months to detect agents that had run amok during internal model training and testing.
Chief executive Sam Altman has joined industry calls to slow the pace of research to ensure AI is developed safely and has said the company has already changed the way it trains models.
Jain said OpenAI faced a “trade-off” between making models persistent enough to complete tasks and ensuring they follow their instructions, a concept known as “alignment”.

“You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction,” Jain said in a statement.
She said GPT-6.1 Astra “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done”.
“When we ship [our models] to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” she added.

A person close to the company said GPT-6.1 Astra had scored below GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s current most advanced model, on alignment evaluations but the company had other models coming soon that met its safety bar. The Wall Street Journal first reported the OpenAI decision.

OpenAI has been reviewing its models’ behaviour during training and evaluation since an incident that came to light in July, in which agents gained access to the internet during testing and hacked into Hugging Face, the AI model and data repository.

The review has so far unearthed several other incidents, including agents hacking an Australian government health service website. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Wednesday called the breach, and OpenAI’s slow response to it, “obviously unacceptable”.

Security breaches at OpenAI and rivals Anthropic and Google have prompted renewed calls for an industry-wide pause or slowdown. Altman joined Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and SpaceX’s Elon Musk in calls to “pace the frontier” of AI development so that safety measures can keep up.

But President Donald Trump has resisted calls to regulate the sector or impose strict guardrails on leading US labs, arguing that American primacy in the technology is vital to staying ahead of China.
Additional reporting by Rafe Rosner-Uddin

title: Anthropic warns of ‘existential risks to humanity’ in IPO prospectus
paragraphs: George Hammondin San Francisco andJames Fontanella-Khanin New York
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
UpdatedSeptember 29 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Anthropic has formally warned investors that its technology may pose “existential risks to humanity” in a long-awaited initial public offering prospectus circulated with a small group of partners in recent days.

The nearly $1tn AI start-up led by Dario Amodei devoted almost a third of its lengthy S1 filing to detailing “risk factors”, including the potential of increasingly advanced AI models to manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other unpredictable behaviours.

Anthropic outlined more prosaic risks, including the extreme concentration of its customer base, with close to a quarter of revenue last year coming from just two clients, according to people familiar with the filing.

The extraordinary warnings in its risk disclosures add to the challenge faced by public markets investors in valuing the leading US AI group when it launches what is expected to be the most highly valued IPO of all time.
The Claude maker also provided investors with a clearer picture of the challenging economics of building state of the art AI models ahead of the listing, expected on the Nasdaq this autumn.
Anthropic said it plans to spend $518bn on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years to support its rapid growth.

The AI lab’s backers are confident Anthropic can list at a valuation of over $2tn, more than double the level achieved in its last funding round in May and beyond the $1.78tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. They point to its extraordinary growth rate to justify their bullishness.
But concerns about the risks posed by AI now threaten to dim that optimism after current and former Anthropic staff came out with public warnings that runaway AI could end humanity within a decade.
Amodei told the UN Security Council last week that AI could threaten humankind and was “the most important global security issue facing the world today”.

The Anthropic chief has this month led public calls for “pacing the frontier” of AI development. His arch-rival at OpenAI, Sam Altman, along with Musk, backed Amodei’s proposals for industry co-operation to slow development and enhance safety measures, in a rare moment of unity.

Safety concerns have increased following a series of high-profile cyber security incidents in which AI ‘agents’ have breached external systems. Last week, OpenAI revealed its tools hadhacked “dozens”of external sites, including governments.
The ChatGPT maker on Mondayscrapped plansto release its newest model next month, citing safety concerns.

Anthropic’s prospectus also revealed details of its prior financial performance and governance arrangements, which were first reported by Reuters and confirmed to the FT by multiple people who have seen the filing.
Anthropic declined to comment.

The company recorded an operating loss of more than $8bn last year as it jacked up spending on computing power, Anthropic told investors. Its revenue jumped twelvefold to almost $4.6bn last year. But mounting costs for computing resources to train and run its models pushed operating expenses to almost $13bn.
The group has inked deals to secure computing power from partners including Google, SpaceX and a series of smaller companies.

Anthropic’s spending and revenue have both increased sharply this year. Revenue in the second quarter of this year was $11.5bn, and it is on course for its second consecutive quarter ofoperating profit, albeit on an adjusted basis.
